question.text: Does ultrasound imaging before puncture facilitate internal jugular vein cannulation?
question.context: To investigate whether prepuncture ultrasound evaluation of vascular anatomy facilitates internal jugular vein cannulation compared with landmark-guided puncture. Prospective randomized study. Single community hospital. Adult patients undergoing general anesthesia (n = 240). The right internal jugular vein was cannulated using either anatomic landmarks or prepuncture ultrasound (3.75/7.5 MHz) guidance. In the landmark group, respiratory jugular venodilation was used as the primary landmark for locating the vein. Results of cannulation and the incidence of complications were compared. Patients were randomly assigned to the ultrasound or landmark group. Respiratory jugular venodilation was identified in 188 patients (78.3%), in whom results of cannulation did not differ between the 2 techniques with respect to the venous access rate (cannulated at the first attempt: 83.5% in the landmark v 85.7% in the ultrasound group), the success rate (cannulated within 3 attempts: 96.9% v 95.6%), and the incidence of arterial puncture (1.0% v 3.3%). In the remaining 52 respiratory jugular venodilation-unidentified patients, the access rate (30.4% v 86.2%, p<0.001) and the success rate (78.3 v 100%, p<0.05) were significantly better in the ultrasound group, and no arterial puncture was recorded in the ultrasound group, whereas the incidence was 13.0% in the landmark group. The results were similar regardless of the ultrasound frequency used.

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The study demonstrates that prepuncture ultrasound guidance significantly improves the success rate and reduces the incidence of arterial puncture compared to landmark-guided puncture. This indicates that ultrasound facilitates internal jugular vein cannulation.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: The results were significantly better in the ultrasound group regarding access rate (30.4% v 86.2%, p<0.001) and success rate (78.3 v 100%, p<0.05) when respiratory jugular venodilation was not identified.
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: While the study focuses on internal jugular vein cannulation, other vascular access routes (e.g., subclavian, femoral) might have different outcomes with ultrasound guidance. However, the primary focus is on internal jugular vein cannulation, and the study's findings strongly support the use of ultrasound.

rnj1_8b.clinical_reasoning: The study demonstrates that ultrasound-guided cannulation significantly improved outcomes in patients with unidentified respiratory jugular venodilation, achieving a 30.4% access rate compared to 86.2% in the landmark group. The ultrasound group also had no arterial puncture incidents versus 13.0% in the landmark group, indicating superior safety and efficacy.
rnj1_8b.critical_evidence: The 30.4% vs 86.2% access rate difference in unidentified venodilation cases with p<0.001 significance
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: No major differential diagnoses needed as the study directly compares the two techniques. The significant improvement in both access rate and safety (no arterial puncture) in the ultrasound group for unidentified venodilation cases provides clear evidence for its superiority.

qwen3_vl_8b.clinical_reasoning: Ultrasound guidance significantly improved cannulation success rates and reduced arterial puncture in patients where respiratory venodilation was not identifiable, which is a common clinical challenge. The data show a clear advantage of ultrasound in this subgroup, making it the best option overall despite similar outcomes in the majority of patients.
qwen3_vl_8b.critical_evidence: In the 52 patients without respiratory venodilation, ultrasound group had 86.2% first-attempt success vs 30.4% in landmark group (p<0.001) and 0% arterial puncture vs 13.0% in landmark group.
qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: Landmark-based technique was considered but ruled out as inferior in patients without visible venodilation. No other imaging modality was compared, so ultrasound was the only alternative evaluated.

olmo3_7b.differential_considered: Other techniques (e.g., femoral vein, axillary approach) might be alternatives, but the study specifically compares internal jugular vein cannulation success and safety between ultrasound and landmark methods, and ultrasound is superior in this context.
